summary: Learners (ages 11–14) build precise command of multiplicative-reasoning vocabulary — direct proportion, inverse proportion, ratio, rate, unit rate, compound unit, scale factor — by USING each term accurately to describe real situations and stating the units a rate/compound measure carries. The goal is correct use in context, not reciting glossary definitions. The two persistent trouble spots are 'proportion' (whose everyday sense 'a large proportion' drifts from the mathematical multiplicative meaning) and the direct/inverse pair (learners label anything with 'more' as 'direct'). Vocabulary is taught with examples AND non-examples tied to situations, and rehearsed in speaking and writing.
misconceptions: Using 'proportion' in its loose everyday sense ('a large proportion') rather than the mathematical multiplicative meaning.
Labelling any 'more → more' situation 'direct proportion' and failing to identify inverse proportion (more workers → less time).
Using 'rate', 'speed' or 'density' without units, or treating 'ratio' and 'rate' as interchangeable.
Confusing 'scale factor' with an additive change rather than a multiplier.

activities.title: Talk it through with a market-stall trader (or science reporter)
steps: Respond in-role to a character who throws real situations at you and listens for the right word: '3 apples for £1 — what do we call this, and what are its units?' (target: it is a rate; its unit rate is 'pounds per apple', found by sharing £1 across 3 apples ≈ £0.33 per apple — or equivalently 3 apples per pound).

When you label 'more workers, fewer hours' as direct, answer the follow-up: 'I add two workers and the time drops — are those two quantities moving the SAME way or opposite?' and revise to 'opposite — and if every worker works at the same rate, doubling the workers halves the time (workers × hours stays constant), so it is INVERSE proportion.'
Describe at least one directly proportional situation, one inverse, and name a rate aloud WITH its units (e.g. '120 miles in 2 hours is 60 miles per hour — a rate/speed, miles per hour').
Say a full sentence that explains WHY, e.g. 'as the petrol increases, the cost increases with it in a constant ratio, so it is direct proportion.'
activities.insight: A term is pinned to the behaviour it names — you decide 'direct' vs 'inverse' by checking whether the quantities move together in a constant ratio (direct) or oppositely with a constant product, so doubling one halves the other (inverse), not by spotting the word 'more'. If neither holds, the relationship is not proportional. A rate is incomplete without its units.

activities.title: Sort-and-tag: direct / inverse / neither, with unit tags
steps: Sort situation cards into three bins: direct proportion, inverse proportion, and neither (non-proportional).
Attach the correct unit tag to each rate card (speed = mph or m/s; density = kg/m³).
Complete sentence frames using the vocabulary, e.g. 'as … increases, … so this is … proportion.'
Read the feedback that names the tell ('both increase together in a constant ratio → direct') and re-sort any you placed wrongly.
activities.insight: The boundary between direct, inverse, and non-proportional situations becomes visible through contrasting examples and non-examples; every rate carries units.

activities.title: Frayer-style term map (reference and consolidation)
steps: For each term (direct proportion, inverse proportion, ratio, rate, unit rate, compound unit, scale factor), fill a four-box map: definition, characteristics, an example, and a non-example.
Add the units for each rate/compound measure (speed: mph or m/s; density: kg/m³).
Explicitly contrast the everyday sense of 'proportion' (an amount) with the mathematical sense (a multiplicative part-to-whole relationship / constant ratio).
Note that 'scale factor' is a MULTIPLIER, not an additive change.
activities.insight: Each term has a fenced meaning with clear examples, non-examples, and (for rates) units; 'proportion' and 'scale factor' have specific mathematical senses distinct from loose everyday use.

activities.title: Check and probe: use the words, generate your own examples
steps: Given two situations — (1) the more workers dig the trench, the less time it takes (assume every worker digs at the same rate); (2) the more petrol you buy, the more it costs (at a fixed price per litre) — state for EACH whether the quantities are in direct or inverse proportion and say a sentence explaining why.
For a car travelling 120 miles in 2 hours, state what '60 miles per hour' is called and what makes it that (a rate/speed, a compound unit comparing distance to time, miles PER hour).
Generate your OWN fresh example of an inverse proportion and your own example of a direct proportion.
Distinguish 'rate' from 'ratio': a rate is a ratio of two DIFFERENT quantities carrying units (X per Y).
activities.insight: Real command shows in how you USE the words in an explaining sentence and in whether you can PRODUCE a correct fresh example — not in label-matching.

checkQuestion: Here are two situations. (1) The more workers dig the trench, the less time it takes. (2) The more petrol you buy, the more it costs. For EACH one, tell me whether the two quantities are in direct proportion or inverse proportion, and say a sentence explaining why. Then: a car travels 120 miles in 2 hours — what do we call the '60 miles per hour', and what makes it that?
checkAnswer: (1) Inverse proportion — as the number of workers increases, the time DEcreases (one goes up as the other goes down). (2) Direct proportion — as the petrol increases, the cost increases with it (both go up together, in a constant ratio). '60 miles per hour' is a RATE (a compound unit/speed), because it compares distance to time — miles PER hour.
